```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

bbs <- read.csv("../data/BBS/FL_BBS.csv")

n_routes_by_year <- tapply(bbs$Route, bbs$Year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })
bob_all <- bbs[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus", ]
n_occ_by_year <- tapply(bob_all$Route, bob_all$Year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })

occ <- data.frame(year = as.numeric(names(n_routes_by_year)),
                  n_routes = as.vector(n_routes_by_year),
                  n_occupied = as.vector(n_occ_by_year))
occ <- occ[occ$n_routes > 10, ]
occ$elapsed <- occ$year - min(occ$year)
occ$prop <- occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes

logit_nll <- function(a, b){
  p <- plogis(a + b * occ$elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
fit_logit <- optim(par = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
                   fn = function(p){ logit_nll(p["a"], p["b"]) },
                   method = "BFGS")

lin_nll <- function(a, b){
  p <- a + b * occ$elapsed
  if (any(p <= 0 | p >= 1)) { return(1e6) }
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
fit_lin <- optim(par = c(a = 0.9, b = -0.008),
                 fn = function(p){ lin_nll(p["a"], p["b"]) },
                 method = "BFGS")

const_fit <- optimize(function(p){
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}, interval = c(0, 1))

y_bob <- bob_all$total_sightings
u_bob <- bob_all$frac_built

urban_nll <- function(mu0, b, size){
  mu <- mu0 * exp(b * u_bob)
  -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}
fit_urban <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                   fn = function(p){ urban_nll(p["mu0"], p["b"], p["size"]) },
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(0.1, -20, 0.05), upper = c(100, 20, 50))

year_bob <- bob_all$Year - min(bob_all$Year)
trend_fit <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 15, decline = 0.03, size = 1),
                   fn = function(p){
                     mu <- p["mu0"] * (1 - p["decline"])^year_bob
                     -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mu, size = p["size"], log = TRUE))
                   },
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(0.1, -0.5, 0.05), upper = c(100, 0.5, 50))

flat_fit <- optimize(function(s){
  -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mean(y_bob), size = s, log = TRUE))
}, interval = c(0.05, 50))
```

## Today's agenda {.smaller}

- Tuesday: up to three parameters at once, each one a single number
- Today: a parameter that **changes from one observation to the next**
- The trick that keeps the optimizer alive
- Two case studies on Florida bobwhite: **where** they are and **how many**

. . .

[Type and run]{.type-badge} on a code block: type it into your script and run it.
You will need it later. Code without the label is there to watch.

::: {.notes}
Chapter 6.3. The shortest new idea in the chapter, and the one that turns
likelihood from a curiosity into the thing you will actually use on your own
data.

The contrast is not how many parameters. Tuesday ended on a three-parameter fit.
It is that every one of them was a single number applied to every observation
equally: one mu for all 1,360 counts, one size for all of them. Real questions
are almost never like that. They ask whether something changes with time, with
habitat, with size, with treatment.

Say it that way if anyone pushes back, because someone will remember fitting mu
and size together and think today is only about adding parameters.
:::

## Where we are {.smaller}

| Section | Question | When |
|---|---|---|
| 6.1 - 6.2 | What parameter values make my data most likely? | Tuesday |
| **6.3** | **What if the parameter depends on a covariate?** | **Today** |
| 6.4 - 6.5 | How sure am I about that parameter? | Next Tuesday |
| 6.6 | Which of two models is better? | Next Thursday |

. . .

Today is the last **mechanical** piece. After this, everything is about how much
to trust the answer.

::: {.notes}
Worth saying out loud: the machinery stops growing today. From here on we are
putting error bars and tests around the same optim() call they already know.
:::

## You already did this {.smaller}

Tuesday's last exercise, the one that estimated the decline:

```{r}
#| eval: false
trend_nll <- function(mu0, decline, size){
  mu <- mu0 * (1 - decline)^year        # <- this line
  -sum(dnbinom(counts, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}
```

. . .

**`mu` is not a number there. It is 1,360 numbers**, one per route-year,
each computed from a covariate.

That is the whole of 6.3.

::: {.notes}
Deliberately a callback, and worth pausing on. Several people got that exercise
working on Tuesday without realizing they had just fit a model with a covariate,
which is the thing the book spends a section on.

Point at the line and ask what mu is. Someone will say "the mean". Then ask how
long it is. That is the moment.
:::

## The recipe {.center}

The **deterministic function** says what the parameter should be.

The **distribution** says how far the data can fall from it.

## Chapter 3 inside Chapter 4 {.smaller}

| Piece | Chapter | Today's first example |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic function | 3 | $p$ falls smoothly with year |
| Distribution | 4 | routes occupied $\sim$ Binomial($n$, $p$) |
| Parameters | 6 | the numbers in the curve: $a$ and $b$ |

. . .

In code it is always these three lines:

```{r}
#| eval: false
nll <- function(parameters){
  predicted <- some_curve(covariate, parameters)      # chapter 3
  -sum(ddist(data, predicted, log = TRUE))            # chapter 4
}
```

::: {.notes}
They have met both halves separately. The only new thing is that the first line
feeds the second.

The third table row is chapter 6, which is not part of the combining: it is where
the numbers in the curve come from, and it is what we are doing today.

Say explicitly: nothing about the optimizer changes. optim() does not know or
care whether the function you hand it has a covariate inside.
:::

## Today's question {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}
![](figures/northern_bobwhite.jpg)

[*Colinus virginianus*]{style="font-size:0.7em"}<br>
[Photo: USFWS, public domain]{style="font-size:0.45em; color:#777"}
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
Tuesday left us two numbers for this bird:

- counts fall about **2.9% a year**, from the trend model you fitted
- **52 of the 71 routes** surveyed in 2019 held bobwhite, so $\hat{p} = 0.73$

. . .

The first used all 23 years. The second used one.

. . .

**Is the share of routes holding bobwhite falling too, and how fast?**
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The point of putting both numbers up is that they answer different questions.
The trend model asked how many birds are on a route. Today asks whether a route
has any at all. Occupancy and abundance, and we do both halves today.

Restate the 52 of 71 in full, because it is the anchor: 71 routes were surveyed
in 2019, and bobwhite were detected on 52 of them.

The honest criticism of that second number is that it threw away 22 years of data
to answer a question about change, which is what today fixes.

If someone asks why we would bother, given that Tuesday already found a decline:
the counts file holds no zeros, so a route that lost its bobwhite entirely simply
vanishes from it. The trend model could not see disappearance. This one can. That
comes back at the end of class, so do not spend long on it here.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
bbs <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/BBS/FL_BBS.csv")

# how many routes were surveyed each year
n_routes_by_year <- tapply(bbs$Route, bbs$Year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })

# how many of them had bobwhite
bob_all <- bbs[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus", ]
n_occ_by_year <- tapply(bob_all$Route, bob_all$Year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })

occ <- data.frame(year = as.numeric(names(n_routes_by_year)),
                  n_routes = as.vector(n_routes_by_year),
                  n_occupied = as.vector(n_occ_by_year))

occ <- occ[occ$n_routes > 10, ]           # 1996 had a single route: drop it
occ$elapsed <- occ$year - min(occ$year)   # 0, 1, 2, ... 22

head(occ)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Two or three minutes for the download. Anyone who still has bbs loaded from
Tuesday can skip the first line.

Should give 23 rows, 1997 through 2019, with n_routes between 64 and 87.

The 1996 row is real, but it has exactly one route in it, so the proportion is 1
out of 1. Ask why that is a problem: a single route tells us almost nothing, yet
the binomial will treat it as a data point like any other. Dropping it is a
judgment call, and the habit worth teaching is making that call visible in the
code instead of silently.

Why elapsed rather than the raw year: with 1997 as a covariate value, the
intercept would mean "logit occupancy in year zero", which is two thousand years
of extrapolation, and the two parameters end up strongly correlated.
:::

## What 23 years look like {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 7.6
plot(occ$year, occ$prop, pch = 16, cex = 1.3, col = "grey25",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "year", ylab = "proportion of routes with bobwhite")
abline(h = const_fit$minimum, col = "grey70", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
text(2012, const_fit$minimum + 0.07, "one number for all 23 years",
     col = "grey45", cex = 0.85)
```

About **0.91** in 1997, about **0.73** in 2019. The dashed line ignores year
entirely: a single $p$, for every route in every year.

::: {.notes}
Let them look before any model. The decline is visible without statistics, which
is the right order: the model quantifies it, it does not discover it.

Point out the wobble too. 2010 is back up at 0.82 and 2008 is down at 0.71.
Nobody should expect a curve to pass through every point.
:::

## The one-number answer, and what it costs {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
const_nll <- function(p){
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

const_fit <- optimize(const_nll, interval = c(0, 1))

c(p = const_fit$minimum, nll = const_fit$objective)
```
:::

. . .

You get $p =$ `r round(const_fit$minimum, 4)`, which is just 1,359 occupied out
of 1,730 surveyed. **Correct, and useless**: it cannot answer the question we
asked.

. . .

Keep the other number it prints, the negative log-likelihood
**`r round(const_fit$objective, 1)`**. Every model we fit today has to beat it,
and **lower is better**.

::: {.notes}
This is the 52-of-71 binomial from Tuesday, pooled over all 23 years, and the
reason to run it is to have a baseline to beat. Put the 79.9 on the board and
leave it there: the exercise in a few slides asks them to get under it, and it is
the only number they will need to carry forward.

Say "lower is better" out loud. It is obvious once you remember the minus sign in
front of the sum, and not obvious at all in the moment.

Be careful not to call this "what we did Tuesday", because Tuesday also ended on
a model where the mean changed with year. The difference here is not old against
new, it is a parameter held constant against a parameter allowed to vary.

Worth noting that the estimate is again exactly the pooled proportion, as it was
for a single year. Nothing new has happened yet.
:::

## What shape should $p$ take? {.smaller}

$p_t$ is the probability a route holds bobwhite in year $t$, counting from
$t = 0$ in 1997. That is the `elapsed` column you just built.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A straight line**

$$p_t = a + b t$$

$b$ is the change in probability per year, readable as it stands.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A logistic curve**

$$p_t = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a + b t)}}$$

Flattens near 0 and 1, so it can never predict an impossible probability.
:::

::::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-width: 8
tt <- 0:22
plot(occ$elapsed, occ$prop, pch = 16, col = "grey45", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "years since 1997", ylab = "proportion occupied")
lines(tt, fit_lin$par["a"] + fit_lin$par["b"] * tt, col = "#1b7837", lwd = 3)
lines(tt, plogis(fit_logit$par["a"] + fit_logit$par["b"] * tt),
      col = "#762a83", lwd = 3)
legend("bottomleft", c("straight line", "logistic"),
       col = c("#1b7837", "#762a83"), lwd = 3, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

::: {.notes}
Over the range of the data the two curves sit almost on top of each other, which
is the honest situation and the reason this slide exists. Students expect the
"right" curve to look obviously better. It usually does not.

Ask which they would pick before showing the next two slides, and take a show of
hands. Most pick the line because it is simpler, and that is a defensible answer
right up until they try to fit it.
:::

## Why the straight line breaks {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
lin_nll <- function(a, b){
  p <- a + b * occ$elapsed
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# a deliberately bad starting guess
optim(par = c(a = 0.5, b = 0.05),
      fn = function(p){
        lin_nll(p["a"], p["b"])
      },
      method = "BFGS")
```
:::

. . .

```
Error in optim(...) : initial value in 'vmmin' is not finite
In addition: Warning message: NaNs produced
```

::: {.notes}
Have them run it and read the error out loud. Errors students produced on purpose
are much less frightening when they turn up by accident later.

Why it happens: at those starting values, year 22 gives
p = 0.5 + 0.05 * 22 = 1.6. A probability of 1.6 is meaningless, dbinom returns
NaN, the sum is NaN, and optim cannot compare NaN with anything, so it quits
before it starts.

The deeper point, said slowly: this is not a bad guess that a better guess would
fix. A straight line is unbounded, so for any nonzero b there is some t where it
leaves (0, 1), and the optimizer is free to walk there at any step. When it does
converge, it converged by luck.
:::

## Fixing it by transformation {.smaller}

Fit the line in a space with **no edges**, then squeeze the result into
$(0, 1)$:

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = a + b t \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a + b t)}}$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-width: 8.4
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 2.0, 0.6), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))
tt2 <- seq(-40, 90, length.out = 300)
plot(tt2, fit_logit$par["a"] + fit_logit$par["b"] * tt2, type = "l", lwd = 3,
     col = "#762a83", xlab = "t, extended far past the data",
     ylab = "log odds of occupancy", main = "a straight line here")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey80", lty = 3)
rect(0, -10, 22, 10, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.06), border = NA)
text(11, -2.6, "the data", cex = 0.8, col = "grey40")
plot(tt2, plogis(fit_logit$par["a"] + fit_logit$par["b"] * tt2), type = "l",
     lwd = 3, col = "#762a83", ylim = c(-0.08, 1.08),
     xlab = "t, extended far past the data",
     ylab = "probability of occupancy", main = "is a curve here")
abline(h = c(0, 1), col = "grey60", lty = 2)
rect(0, -1, 22, 2, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.06), border = NA)
text(11, 0.12, "the data", cex = 0.8, col = "grey40")
```

::: {.notes}
The left panel runs from about minus one to plus three, and could run to a
million without anything going wrong. The right panel is the same line, and it
cannot leave the box no matter what a and b do. That is the entire argument.

Name the pieces: the quantity on the left is the log odds, also called the logit.
R calls the squeezing function plogis() and the unsqueezing function qlogis().
They are the p and q functions of the logistic distribution, from the same d, p,
q, r family as everything else this semester.
:::

## Meet `plogis()` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
plogis(c(-3, -1, 0, 1, 3))   # log odds  ->  probability

qlogis(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))     # probability  ->  log odds

plogis(500)                  # however large the input, never above 1
```
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(log_odds = c(-3, -1, 0, 1, 3),
                        probability = round(plogis(c(-3, -1, 0, 1, 3)), 3)))
```

::: {.notes}
Three things from the table: zero on the log odds scale is a probability of one
half, the function is symmetric about that point, and the two ends flatten out
instead of running off.

The last line is the one to dwell on. plogis(500) returns 1, not something
larger, and that is the property this whole slide exists for: there is no value
of a + b * t, however extreme, that this function can turn into an illegal
probability. That is what makes the optimizer safe.

If a fitted parameter ever does send you out to 500, the model is telling you the
data hold no counter-examples at all, which is worth noticing rather than
ignoring.
:::

## Writing the likelihood {.smaller}

Three steps, and only the first is new:

```{r}
#| eval: false
occ_nll <- function(a, b){

  # 1. turn the two parameters into a probability for every year
  # 2. ask dbinom how likely the observed counts are, on the log scale
  # 3. add them up and flip the sign

}
```

. . .

Step 1 is `plogis(a + b * occ$elapsed)`.

Steps 2 and 3 are **exactly what you wrote on Tuesday**, unchanged.

::: {.notes}
The body is deliberately empty, because the next slide is theirs. The only thing
worth giving away is that the covariate enters in step 1 and nothing downstream
changes.

If anyone asks why the function takes a and b separately instead of a vector:
good question, and we switch to a vector in twenty minutes for a reason.
:::

## Your turn: fit the decline {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
occ_nll <- function(a, b){
  p <- plogis(a + b * occ$elapsed)
  # your negative log-likelihood goes here
  # (dbinom wants x, size and prob: which column of occ is which?)
}

fit_occ <- optim(par = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
                 fn = function(p){
                   # call your NLL here, with the two parameters
                 },
                 method = "BFGS")

fit_occ$par
fit_occ$value
```
:::

**Is your `b` negative? And is `fit_occ$value` below 79.9**, the negative
log-likelihood of the single-$p$ model?

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes. Both missing pieces are recall rather than syntax.

The body is
-sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
and the wrapper is occ_nll(p["a"], p["b"]).

One trap worth letting them hit: all three dbinom arguments come from occ, and
swapping n_occupied for n_routes gives an immediate NaN, because x cannot exceed
size. That error message is informative.

The answer: a = 2.018, b = -0.0619, NLL 56.69. Anyone who gets 56.69 has it.

Point anyone stuck back at Tuesday's "Fitting it" slide rather than telling them.
Mention that the p inside the optim wrapper and the p inside occ_nll are
different objects, which is confusing, and which is exactly why real code passes
its data in explicitly.
:::

## What the answer means {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = c("a", "b"),
  estimate = round(unname(c(fit_logit$par["a"], fit_logit$par["b"])), 4),
  meaning = c("log odds of occupancy in 1997",
              "change in log odds per year")))
```

- $a = 2.02$ is on the log odds scale, so occupancy in 1997 was
  `plogis(2.02)` = **`r round(plogis(fit_logit$par["a"]), 2)`**
- $b = -0.062$ is **not** percentage points. `exp(-0.0619)` =
  `r round(exp(fit_logit$par["b"]), 3)`, so the **odds fall about 6% per year**
- By 2019 the curve is down to
  **`r round(plogis(fit_logit$par["a"] + 22 * fit_logit$par["b"]), 2)`**

. . .

**If you fit on a transformed scale, you have to transform back before you can
say what the answer means.** The optimizer works in log odds. Nobody thinks in
log odds. The same holds in the second half of today, with `exp()` in place of
`plogis()`.

::: {.notes}
The interpretation slide matters more than the fitting slide. A student who
reports b = -0.062 as "a 6% decline in occupancy" has made a real error: the 6%
is a change in odds, not in probability, and the two only agree when p is small.

Work one through on the board. Odds in 1997 are 0.88 / 0.12, about 7.5 to 1. In
2019 they are 0.66 / 0.34, about 1.9 to 1. Multiplying 7.5 by 0.94 twenty-two
times gives 1.9.

This is the single most common misreading of a logistic fit in the published
literature, so it is worth the three minutes.

The last line is the one to make them write down, because it generalizes past
today. Transforming is how we kept the optimizer legal, and the price of that
convenience is that the number which comes back is in the transformed currency.
It stays meaningless until converted. Call back to it in the second half, when
exp() turns a log-scale slope into "half the birds per 21% developed", and again
in Lecture 24 when glm() does the transforming for them and quietly hands back
coefficients on the link scale.
:::

## Check it by plotting {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
plot(occ$elapsed, occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes, pch = 16,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "years since 1997", ylab = "proportion occupied")

elapsed_seq <- 0:22

lines(elapsed_seq,
      plogis(fit_occ$par["a"] + fit_occ$par["b"] * elapsed_seq),
      col = "red", lwd = 3)
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 7
plot(occ$elapsed, occ$prop, pch = 16, col = "grey30", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "years since 1997", ylab = "proportion occupied")
lines(0:22, plogis(fit_logit$par["a"] + fit_logit$par["b"] * (0:22)),
      col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

::: {.notes}
The habit from Tuesday, and the one that catches the most mistakes: fitted
parameters plugged back into the equation, drawn over the data.

If the line misses the cloud entirely, the usual cause is forgetting the
back-transformation, that is, plotting a + b * t instead of plogis(a + b * t).
That mistake produces a line from 2 to 0.6 on a 0 to 1 axis, which looks almost
plausible, which is why it is worth naming.
:::

## Was the trend worth fitting? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = c("one p for all years", "p declines with year"),
  parameters = c(1, 2),
  NLL = round(c(const_fit$objective, fit_logit$value), 2)))
```

**`r round(const_fit$objective - fit_logit$value, 1)` log-likelihood units** for
one extra parameter.

. . .

Is 23 units enough to justify a parameter? **That is next Thursday.** For now:
clearly yes, and we will learn how to say so properly.

::: {.notes}
Same move as Tuesday. Give them the comparison they want, name the number, and
be explicit that the machinery for judging it comes later.

Anyone who remembers Tuesday's Poisson against negative binomial comparison,
which was thousands of units, will see that this one is far smaller but still
large. The scale will get meaning next Thursday: twice the difference, compared
against a chi-squared with one degree of freedom, so the threshold is about 1.92
units. 23 clears it comfortably.
:::

## What about that straight line? {.smaller}

Stop it from proposing illegal probabilities and it fits perfectly well. In fact
it fits **slightly better**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  shape = c("straight line, guarded", "logistic"),
  parameters = c(2, 2),
  NLL = round(c(fit_lin$value, fit_logit$value), 2)))
```

. . .

So why not use it?

- `r round(abs(fit_lin$value - fit_logit$value), 2)` units on 23 points is
  **nothing**,
  and next Thursday gives us the test to say so
- it only fits at all because we hand-wrote a guard around it
- run it to 2100 and it predicts an occupancy of
  **`r round(fit_lin$par["a"] + 103 * fit_lin$par["b"], 2)`**

. . .

**Fit is one criterion. It is not the only one.**

::: {.notes}
The slide that keeps the earlier argument honest. Students who picked the line on
the show of hands were not being silly, and they deserve to see that their choice
loses on grounds other than fit.

The guard is one line added to lin_nll:

  if (any(p <= 0 | p >= 1)) { return(1e6) }

which tells the optimizer "do not go there" by making it look terrible. It works,
and it is a hack: the surface it is optimizing now has a cliff in it, the answer
depends on the penalty you chose, and nothing warns you if the fitted line is
sitting right against the edge.

The negative probability in 2100 is the part to linger on. Within the data the
two shapes are indistinguishable, so the choice is entirely about what the model
claims outside the range you measured. That is where a model earns or loses
trust, and it is invisible in any goodness-of-fit number.

If someone asks which they should use in their own project: whichever one cannot
produce an impossible value. That rule has never cost anybody anything.
:::

## You just built a GLM by hand {.smaller}

```{r}
glm(cbind(n_occupied, n_routes - n_occupied) ~ elapsed,
    data = occ, family = binomial)$coefficients
```

. . .

The same two numbers, to three decimals. A **binomial GLM** is exactly what you
just wrote: a logistic curve inside a binomial likelihood.

. . .

So why write it by hand? Because `glm()` knows a short list of shapes, and
**the next case study is not on the list.**

::: {.notes}
Worth the payoff, and worth the honesty. They have reinvented something with a
one-line interface, and in Lecture 24 they get the one-line interface.

The reason to do it the long way, which is Bolker's whole argument: glm() offers
a small menu of deterministic functions, all of them straight lines pushed
through a link. The moment your biology suggests a saturating curve, a threshold
or an optimum, the menu runs out and you are back to writing the likelihood
yourself. The second half of today is an example.

If anyone asks about the tiny difference in the fourth decimal: glm uses a
specialized algorithm rather than general-purpose optim, so its answer is the
more accurate one.
:::

## Keeping parameters legal {.smaller}

| The parameter must be | Fit this instead | Get back with |
|---|---|---|
| a probability in $(0,1)$ | the log odds | `plogis()` |
| positive: `sd`, `size`, a rate | its logarithm | `exp()` |
| unconstrained | itself | nothing |

. . .

This is why the book writes things like `sd = exp(params[3])`. It is not a
statistical statement. It is a fence to keep the optimizer out of the region
where the likelihood is undefined.

::: {.notes}
Three lines of table that will save them hours in the final project.

The pattern to recognize: whenever an optimizer returns NaN, Inf, or "non-finite
finite-difference value", the first thing to check is whether some parameter has
wandered somewhere illegal.
:::

## Bounds, or a transformation? {.smaller}

Tuesday we used bounds instead: `method = "L-BFGS-B"`, with `lower` and `upper`.

. . .

| | Use it when |
|---|---|
| **Bounds** | the parameter itself must stay in a range: `size > 0` |
| **Transformation** | a **computed** quantity must stay in range for every observation |

. . .

Today needed the transformation: bounds on $a$ and $b$ cannot guarantee that
$a + bt$ lands inside $(0,1)$ for all 23 years.

::: {.notes}
This distinction is not in the book as such, and it is the one students get
wrong. They reach for bounds first because they met them first.

Make the argument concretely: you could try to bound a and b tightly enough that
a + bt stays legal, but the legal region is a triangle in (a, b) space, not a
box, and optim only understands boxes. The transformation makes every box legal.
:::

## Passing the data in {.smaller}

So far the likelihood reached out and grabbed `occ` from the workspace. Fine in a
lecture, a trap in a project:

```{r}
#| eval: false
occ_nll <- function(a, b){
  p <- plogis(a + b * occ$elapsed)        # where did occ come from?
  ...
}
```

. . .

Change `occ` and the function silently means something different. Better, and the
form `mle2()` expects:

```{r}
#| eval: false
occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
```

::: {.notes}
A software point rather than a statistical one, but it is the bug that will eat
their final project: a function that depends on a global is only correct while
nobody touches the global.

The version taking a params vector is also what the book uses throughout 6.3,
so it is worth seeing both forms side by side before they meet it in the reading.
:::

## The same fit with `mle2()` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(bbmle)

occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")        # mle2 insists on names

m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2,
              start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
              data = list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied,
                          n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                          elapsed = occ$elapsed))

coef(m_occ)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Same answer, third route to it, and the reason to bother is next Tuesday:
summary(m_occ) gives standard errors and confidence intervals that optim does
not hand over as readily.

parnames() is the step everyone forgets. Without it mle2 cannot tell which
element of the vector is which, and the error message is not helpful.
:::

## The book's version of today {.smaller}

Bolker's 6.3 does the same thing with tadpoles and predators:

$$p = \frac{a}{1 + a h N}$$

- $N$ is the number of tadpoles stocked, the covariate
- $a$ is attack rate, $h$ is handling time, the parameters
- the number eaten is **binomial** with that $p$

. . .

Same three lines. A different curve from the Chapter 3 bestiary.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(emdbook)
data(ReedfrogFuncresp)       # if you want to follow the book exactly
```

::: {.notes}
Worth one slide because they read it, and because the final project may well need
a saturating curve.

The biology of the shape: a predator that spends time handling each prey item
cannot keep up as prey get denser, so the per capita predation rate falls with
density even though the total number eaten rises. The same hyperbolic shape they
met in Lecture 9 as Michaelis-Menten.
:::

## Occupancy, or abundance? {.center}

We asked **whether** bobwhite are there.

The counts say **how many**.

## Where are bobwhite still doing well? {.smaller}

Each BBS route carries landscape data, including `frac_built`: the fraction of
the route's surroundings that is developed.

. . .

Bobwhite need **early-succession** habitat: old fields, field edges, pine
savanna kept open by fire.

. . .

**Does the count fall as development rises, and by how much?**

::: {.notes}
A different question from the first half, deliberately, and one with a management
use: it says where the remaining birds are rather than how fast they are going.

Say where frac_built comes from: it is spatial data added to the BBS download,
documented in data/BBS/README. It is a property of the route, measured once, not
a time series. That matters in twenty minutes.
:::

## Get set up, again {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
y_bob <- bob_all$total_sightings    # birds counted on a route in a year
u_bob <- bob_all$frac_built         # fraction developed around that route

length(y_bob)                       # 1360 route-years

plot(u_bob, y_bob, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.25),
     xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "bobwhite counted")
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-width: 7
plot(u_bob, y_bob, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.25),
     xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "bobwhite counted")
```

::: {.notes}
bob_all already exists from the first half, so this is three lines.

The cloud is lopsided: most routes are barely developed, a handful are over 40%
built, and the high counts all live on the left. Ask what the plot alone tells
them before any model: there is clearly something there, and it is clearly not a
straight line.
:::

## Choosing the shape {.smaller}

$\mu$ is the expected count on a route and $u$ its fraction developed, the
`u_bob` you just made. $\mu_0$ is the count where nothing is built.

| Candidate | Equation | The problem with it |
|---|---|---|
| straight line | $\mu = \mu_0 + b u$ | goes negative, and $\mu$ must be positive |
| power law | $\mu = \mu_0 u^{\,b}$ | infinite at $u = 0$, and 78 routes have $u = 0$ |
| **exponential** | $\mu = \mu_0 e^{\,bu}$ | **positive everywhere, finite at zero** |

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.1
#| fig-width: 7.6
uu <- seq(0, 0.5, length.out = 200)
plot(uu, 12 * exp(-3.2 * uu), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83",
     ylim = c(-2, 14), xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "expected count")
lines(uu, 12 - 28 * uu, lwd = 3, col = "#1b7837")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
legend("topright", c("exponential", "straight line"),
       col = c("#762a83", "#1b7837"), lwd = 3, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

::: {.notes}
Same move as the logistic earlier: the choice is made on what the curve can and
cannot do, not on which looks prettier.

The straight line crosses zero around 43% developed, and we have routes past
that. A negative mean is not a slightly wrong answer, it is an undefined one:
dnbinom with a negative mu returns NaN.

The power law is the interesting rejection, because it is the usual choice for
this kind of question and it fails here for a data reason rather than a
mathematical one: 78 route-years sit at exactly zero development.

Interpretation of the parameters: mu0 is the expected count in undeveloped
surroundings, and b is how fast that falls, with b negative for a decline, as in
the first half of today.

Worth making the connection explicit, because it is the same trick twice. Taking
logs of the exponential gives log(mu) = log(mu0) + b * u, so this is again a
straight line on a transformed scale, back-transformed to keep the parameter
legal. The first half used the log odds to keep p inside (0, 1); this half uses
the log to keep mu above zero. That is the "Keeping parameters legal" table, in
use.
:::

## Choosing the distribution {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mean(y_bob)
var(y_bob)
var(y_bob) / mean(y_bob)
```
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean", "variance", "variance / mean"),
  value = round(c(mean(y_bob), var(y_bob), var(y_bob) / mean(y_bob)), 2),
  Poisson_expects = c("", "", "1")))
```

**`r round(var(y_bob)/mean(y_bob), 1)`**, not 1. Counts, overdispersed, so
**negative binomial**, exactly as on Tuesday.

::: {.notes}
A deliberate repeat of Tuesday's diagnostic, because the point is that the
distribution choice and the curve choice are separate decisions made on separate
evidence.

The variance to mean ratio of 10 is the same clumping they found on Tuesday: a
covey is 10 or 12 birds, so a route either has a covey or it does not.
:::

## Your turn: fit the habitat effect {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
urban_nll <- function(mu0, b, size){
  mu <- mu0 * exp(b * u_bob)
  # your negative log-likelihood goes here
  # (three parameters now, and mu is a vector)
}

fit_urban <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                   fn = function(p){
                     # call your NLL here, with the three parameters
                   },
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(0.1, -20, 0.05),
                   upper = c(100, 20, 50))

fit_urban$par
fit_urban$value
```
:::

**What count does your model expect on an undeveloped route? On one that is 20%
developed?**

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes, and the structure is now familiar enough that most will get it in
five.

The body is -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE)) and the
wrapper is urban_nll(p["mu0"], p["b"], p["size"]).

Answers: mu0 = 12.13, b = -3.23, size = 1.48, NLL 4574.1. Negative b, same as
the negative b in the occupancy fit, and for the same reason.

The two predictions are the point of the question, and they should compute them
rather than read them: 12.13 * exp(-3.23 * 0) = 12.1 birds, and
12.13 * exp(-3.23 * 0.2) = 6.4 birds, so a fifth of the landscape developed
costs about half the birds.

Note that size came out at 1.48, against 1.37 for the flat model on Tuesday.
Some of what looked like clumping was really habitat.
:::

## What it means {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 7.2
br <- cut(u_bob, breaks = c(0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1),
          include.lowest = TRUE)
mids <- c(0.01, 0.035, 0.075, 0.15, 0.3, 0.6)
plot(u_bob, y_bob, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.12),
     xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "bobwhite counted", ylim = c(0, 40))
points(mids, tapply(y_bob, br, mean), pch = 17, cex = 1.5, col = "#2166ac")
uu2 <- seq(0, 0.5, length.out = 200)
lines(uu2, fit_urban$par["mu0"] * exp(fit_urban$par["b"] * uu2),
      col = "red", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", c("binned means", "fitted curve"), pch = c(17, NA),
       lty = c(NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, 3), col = c("#2166ac", "red"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

- $\mu_0 =$ **`r round(fit_urban$par["mu0"], 1)`** birds where nothing is built
- `r round(fit_urban$par["mu0"] * exp(fit_urban$par["b"] * 0.2), 1)` birds at
  20% developed, **`r round(fit_urban$par["mu0"] * exp(fit_urban$par["b"] * 0.5), 1)`**
  at 50%
- Halved by **`r round(100 * log(2) / abs(fit_urban$par["b"]), 0)`%** development,
  since $\log(2) / |b|$ = `r round(log(2) / abs(fit_urban$par["b"]), 3)`

::: {.notes}
The blue triangles are binned averages, added only as a check on the curve: they
were not used in the fit, and the curve passes through them.

The halving number is the one to remember, because it is the form a manager can
use: every 21 percentage points of development costs half the birds.

That constant-halving property is what choosing an exponential bought us. It is
the same arithmetic as a half-life.
:::

## Three models, one dataset {.smaller}

All three fit the same 1,360 counts with a negative binomial:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = c("mu is constant",
            "mu declines with year (Tuesday)",
            "mu declines with development (today)"),
  parameters = c(2, 3, 3),
  NLL = round(c(flat_fit$objective, trend_fit$value, fit_urban$value), 1)))
```

. . .

The last two cost the **same** number of parameters, so no test is needed to
compare them: development fits better by
**`r round(trend_fit$value - fit_urban$value, 0)`** units.

::: {.notes}
A clean comparison, and rare: equal parameter counts means lower NLL simply wins,
with none of next Thursday's machinery.

Worth saying what it does and does not mean. It does mean that if you had to
predict the count on an unknown route with one piece of information, you would
rather know its development than its year. It does not mean development causes
the decline, which is the next slide.
:::

## What this cannot tell you {.smaller}

**`frac_built` is measured once per route.** It does not change over the 23 years.

. . .

So it can explain **where** bobwhite are scarce. It cannot explain **why they
declined**: a variable that does not change over time cannot account for a change
over time.

. . .

And the counts file holds only routes where the species was **seen**, so the
zeros are missing. Occupancy had the zeros; abundance has the counts. **You need
both halves**, which is why we fit both.

::: {.notes}
The slide that keeps today honest, and the one most likely to come up in their
own projects.

Check it with them if they are skeptical: cor(bob_all$frac_built, bob_all$Year)
is -0.05, so
development as measured here is essentially unrelated to year. The two models are
answering different questions, not competing for the same explanation.

The missing zeros are a genuine bias and worth naming rather than hiding: mu0 is
too high, because routes where bobwhite were absent contribute no row at all. The
fix is beyond today, but the habit of asking "what rows are missing from this
file" is not.
:::

## What you can now do {.smaller}

- Put a **Chapter 3 curve** inside a **Chapter 4 distribution**
- Transform a constrained parameter so the optimizer stays in legal territory
- Fit it, interpret it on the right scale, and plot it over the data
- Compare two shapes by their negative log-likelihood

. . .

Still missing: **how sure are you about $b$?** That is next Tuesday.

::: {.notes}
Point out that they now have everything needed for Part 2 of most final projects.
The remaining lectures add confidence and comparison, not new fitting machinery.
:::

## Additional practice {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Reef fish richness against depth. Same five steps, less handholding:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
reef <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/Reef_fish/NCRMP_reef_fish_surveys.csv")
depth <- reef$DEPTH
rich <- reef$species_richness
# 1. look first. flat, rising, or humped?
plot(depth, rich, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.05))
# 2. which distribution? run Tuesday's check before you decide
var(rich) / mean(rich)
# 3. a hump needs three numbers: how high, where, and how wide
reef_nll <- function(peak, opt, width, size){
  mu <- peak * exp(-(depth - opt)^2 / (2 * width^2))
  # your negative log-likelihood goes here
}
# 4. four parameters, so bounds are worth having
fit_reef <- optim(par = c(peak = 25, opt = 20, width = 15, size = 10),
                  fn = function(p){
                    # your NLL, with four parameters this time
                  },
                  method = "L-BFGS-B",
                  lower = c(1, 0, 1, 0.1), upper = c(200, 60, 200, 1000))
# 5. plot the curve over the cloud. does it match the hump from step 1?
```
:::

::: {.notes}
For outside class, or for anyone who finishes early. Same shape as today, with
three things deliberately not given: the distribution, the NLL body, and the
optim wrapper.

The curve is a Gaussian shape used as a deterministic function, which is a
different job from a Gaussian used as a distribution. Worth flagging if anyone
asks: peak is the richness at the optimum, opt is the depth of that optimum, and
width controls how fast richness falls away from it.

Answers, for my own reference: peak 24.7 species, opt 16.1 m, width 24.2 m, size
6.5, NLL 31752, against 31799 for a flat model. So the optimum is real but the
hump is very broad, which is the honest finding and a good reminder that a
detectable effect can still be a small one.

They should find var/mean near 4.4, so negative binomial again.
:::
